title: Bites - Animal
changeSummary: Migrated to component-based prescribing regimens; clinical content unchanged.
clinicalNotes: Surgical toilet is most important. Assess tetanus and rabies risk.
Antibiotic prophylaxis advised for cat bites that have broken the skin and drawn blood or broken the skin and not drawn blood if the wound could be deep.

Antibiotic prophylaxis is not required for bites from a dog or other traditional pet (excluding cat bites) that have not broken the skin or have broken the skin but not drawn blood. Antibiotic prophylaxis advised for bites if: it has penetrated bone, joint, tendon, ligament or vascular structures; it is deep, is a puncture or crush wound, or has caused significant tissue damage; it involves high risk area such as hand, foot, face, genitals, skin overlying cartilaginous structures or an area of poor circulation; it is visibly contaminated (e.g. if there is dirt or a tooth in the wound); the person is at risk of a serious wound infection because of a comorbidity, e.g. immunocompromised, diabetes, elderly, cirrhotic or asplenic patients, decompensated liver disease, presence of prosthetic valve or prosthetic joint.
For people with an insect bite or sting who have symptoms or signs of an infection, see the recommendations on choice of antibiotic in Cellulitis & Erysipelas.
Seek specialist advice if person is pregnant.

notes: A 5-day course is appropriate for treating most human or animal bites, but course length can be increased to 7 days (with review) based on clinical assessment of the wound, for example, if there is significant tissue destruction or it has penetrated bone, joint, tendon or vascular structures.

See the BNF, BNF for Children, and summary of product characteristics for appropriate use and dosing in specific populations, for example, for people with hepatic or renal impairment, in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and when administering intravenous (or, if appropriate, intramuscular) antibiotics.
